reasons: Tier 4: moves money with no person confirming (Wire transfer API)
Tier 4: acts with no person confirming (ERP financial system, Vendor invoices email inbox)
Tier 2: can act beyond reading (ERP financial system, Vendor invoices email inbox, Wire transfer API)

summary: This agent is high-risk: it autonomously approves and sends wire transfers (up to $25,000) with no human confirmation and has move_money privileges, persistent shared memory, and processes untrusted email attachments. Immediate mitigations required include disabling autonomous payments, enforcing human approvals, tightening credential scope and model supply-chain controls, partitioning memory, and implementing an automated tested kill switch.

findings.evidenceQuote: approves and initiates wire transfers of up to $25,000 without human review.
findings.whyItMatters: The agent can autonomously approve and send wire transfers with no human in the loop, enabling large unauthorized financial transfers if the agent is compromised or misbehaves.
findings.recommendedControl: Require multi-person manual approval for any wire transfer and disable autonomous move_money actions; implement workflow gating so the agent only drafts payment requests that a human must explicitly authorize.

findings.whyItMatters: The agent has direct privilege to move funds. Coupled with an attached credential, this allows abuse of identity/privilege to perform financial operations without additional checks.
findings.recommendedControl: Scope and restrict the agent's token to least privilege (remove direct move_money), require short-lived credentials with strong authorization checks and auditable service account usage, and enforce transaction limits with independent approval.

findings.whyItMatters: The agent consumes untrusted email input (including attachments) to trigger payments; email-based inputs are a common vector for injection, malformed attachments, or spoofed invoices that could cause fraudulent payments.
findings.recommendedControl: Block autonomous payments from email-derived inputs: require human validation of any invoice originating from email, sanitize and validate attachments, and apply strict vendor identity verification before any payment initiation.

findings.evidenceQuote: It keeps a memory of vendor history to spot anomalies, but that memory store is shared across all vendor accounts with no per-vendor separation.
findings.whyItMatters: A shared persistent memory across vendors allows cross-account contamination or poisoning (e.g., attacker-controlled vendor history influencing payments for other vendors), undermining the agent's anomaly detection.
findings.recommendedControl: Partition the memory store by vendor with access controls and integrity checks, and implement input validation and rate limits plus mechanisms to audit and roll back memory updates.

findings.whyItMatters: A self-hosted, unspecified Llama model may have unpatched vulnerabilities or unknown provenance that introduce supply-chain risks (model compromise or malicious weights).
findings.recommendedControl: Pin and document the exact model/version, validate model integrity (checksums, signatures), keep the runtime patched, and perform an internal security review of the self-hosted model before production use.

findings.evidenceQuote: "description": "Manual: the on-call engineer disables the agent's service account. No tested runbook."
findings.whyItMatters: The kill switch is manual and untested, so during an incident the agent may continue to operate and cause cascading financial damage before it can be reliably disabled.
findings.recommendedControl: Implement an automated, tested emergency stop that immediately blocks the agent's ability to transact (network-level or API gateway kill), document and test a runbook regularly, and ensure on-call staff training and escalation procedures.
